title: Inside a colo
text: Everything in this series meets in one building: the exchange's data centre. Here is how a trading firm's network is laid out inside it.

title: Why co-locate
text: Co-location means renting space for your servers in the same data centre as the matching engine. Nasdaq says round trip latency there, order to acknowledgement, is under 50 microseconds. From ten kilometres away, the fibre alone would add about 100 microseconds to every round trip. Every metre of fibre counts: about 4.9 nanoseconds each.

title: A cabinet and its cross-connects
text: The firm rents a cabinet, and reaches the outside world through cross-connects: Equinix defines them as dedicated, physical cabling links between two parties inside one data centre. Market data arrives from the exchange hand-off on A and B feeds, and a layer 1 switch can copy them to many servers in a few nanoseconds. Orders leave through a low latency switch on a separate path, so a burst of market data never queues in front of them. A PTP clock, steered by GPS, timestamps everything, and taps feed a capture box.

title: A cabinet budget
text: Now add up a tick-to-order path, with the vendor best cases from earlier in this series. A layer 1 fan-out adds 5 nanoseconds, and 10 metres of fibre about 50. The order leaves through a cut-through switch at about 250. What remains is the server: the card, the network stack and your code. With kernel bypass that is around a microsecond or more, so the server is usually the biggest share. So shaving time off the server is usually worth more than shaving the cable.

title: The lab's version
text: The lab builds the same picture inside one machine. simex plays the exchange, publishing its feed on multicast over loopback, instead of across a cross-connect. Feed handler, trader and exchange each get their own cores, and orders return to simex over TCP, in OUCH. The numbers differ, but the shape is the same.

title: What catches firms out
text: Some details catch firms out. Port products differ: Nasdaq says its 10 gigabit Ultra matches its 40 gigabit latency, and cuts round trips by two to five microseconds on average. Equinix cross-connects have been single-mode fibre only since March 2024, so buy optics to match. A microwave link needs a fibre backup, because rain is the most common cause of outages. And one feed, one switch or one clock is a single point of failure, so keep the A and B paths apart.

title: The series in one line
text: Multicast in, TCP out, no kernel in the way, hardware clocks, few hops, short queues. Measure every hop, and keep the clocks honest. That is a trading network, from the wire to the matching engine.
